claims.text: The starting catalyst is a nearly equiatomic multi-element high-entropy alloy with low platinum content.
The starting catalyst loses activity and degrades upon exposure to H2O, NO, and thermal aging under automotive exhaust conditions.
Post-synthesis thermal treatment in a nitrogen-containing atmosphere can dope the catalyst surface with nitrogen.
The nitrogen-containing thermal treatment will drive segregation of a thin platinum-enriched shell over the bulk high-entropy alloy.
The resulting Pt-rich surface will contain numerous stabilizing metal–nitrogen bonds.
Chemically stable metal–nitrogen bonds suppress dissolution and oxidation of transition metals.
Nitrogen-induced modification of the electronic structure of surface Pt inhibits dissolution of the Pt shell.
Nitrogen doping produces local lattice distortion that can suppress metal-atom diffusion and enhance durability.
The nitrogen-stabilized Pt-rich layer prevents agglomeration of Pt atoms.
The stabilized Pt-rich shell will mitigate Pt leaching and activity loss during corrosive exhaust exposure and thermal cycling.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the intervention will improve catalytic activity retention and durability during transient exhaust exposure and thermal aging.
The intervention will maintain low platinum-group-metal consumption.
Cycling between 100°C and 300°C with intermittent H2O and NO exposure represents the intended transient, low-temperature aging environment.
The untreated control shows rapid activity loss and limited durability in water- and NO-containing transient exhaust.
The intervention's performance at high temperature or under markedly different operating conditions is unverified.
The magnitude of improvement and optimal nitrogen concentration and treatment duration remain to be established experimentally.
A controlled 100-hour comparison under 100–300°C cycling with H2O and NO can test activity retention, Pt loss, and structural stability.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in activity retention, Pt dissolution, or structural stability relative to the untreated control would falsify the hypothesis.
